name: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital: patient care, St. Jude Global, training and community programmes (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: St. Jude Global's partner hospitals in more than 70 countries and the graduate school's research (89% of the result at the defaults, spread by world population: a judgment, the build names no split), and patient care, clinical training and community programmes in the US (11%).
summary: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis treats about 1,000 new patients a year with childhood cancer and other catastrophic diseases, free to families, supports children's cancer care at partner hospitals in more than 70 countries through St. Jude Global, and trains clinicians and scientists and runs community health programmes. For its fiscal year to June 2025 these come to about 0.004 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.0004 to 0.04), far below the site's global-health median (about a thousandth of it). St. Jude Global, 14% of the cost, brings nearly nine-tenths of the result: partner hospitals in middle-income countries save more children per improvement, but they and their governments carry most of the cost of treatment, so St. Jude's share of the credit is about a fifth, and the gain rests on before-and-after results at a few flagship sites. US care is lower still: about $1 million of St. Jude's own money per new patient buys a few points of survival over the other US centres these children would otherwise attend. Every branch (patient care, St. Jude Global, clinical training, the graduate school, community programmes) is discounted for missing data, since St. Jude publishes no controlled outcome for any of them; training and the community programmes are built from the research on training and on HPV vaccination promotion. The result is mostly uncertainty, above all whether St. Jude Global's support changes survival at partner hospitals at all.

rows.label: Share of the hospital's education and training that is St. Jude Global
rows.explainer: Judgment. The hospital's Form 990 says St. Jude Global's 'financial support will grow to $100 million annually by 2024' (Schedule H, Part VI, FY2024 return); its education and training line was $113.6 million that year and $146.2 million in FY2025, so Global (its Global Alliance, twinning with partner hospitals, training of partners' staff and the $200 million Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines run with WHO) is most of it: $105 million of $146 million at the best guess. The rest is the graduate school, fellowships, K-12 science programmes and community health work in Memphis, the training and community branches below (tr_, gs_, cm_). Low if Global stayed at $80 million; high if nearly all growth went to Global and the Platform. St. Jude's launch release for St. Jude Global (May 2018) announced it was 'investing more than $100 million' in the initiative (https://www.stjude.org/media-resources/news-releases/2018-medicine-science-news/st-jude-expands-international-reach-with-st-jude-global.html), a cross-check on the 990's figure, which is in a scanned return.

rows.explainer: About $41 million: clinical fellowships and residencies, nurse and allied-health training, the St. Jude Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, and the Memphis community health programmes (HPV vaccination, HIV education, school health lessons, survivorship and transition support). The hospital's Form 990 reported $21.8 million for education and training in FY2018, before St. Jude Global's growth, a cross-check on the size of these programmes. St. Jude reports activities but no outcomes for them, so each is built from the research on its kind of work (Convention 12).

rows.label: Community health programmes' share of that spending
rows.explainer: Judgment. The Community Health Needs Assessment 2022 (https://www.stjude.org/content/dam/en_US/shared/www/patient-support/sjcrh-chna-report-2022.pdf, pp. 51-52) lists the community benefit work: the HPV Cancer Prevention Program (partner mailings, a monthly newsletter to 800 partners, provider seminars, the Memphis-Shelby County and southeastern HPV roundtables), 65 HIV education sessions reaching 6,100 people (FY2020), healthy-lifestyle lessons for 2,000 Memphis K-12 students (2018-19), tele-mental-health referrals for caregivers and transition programmes. Small teams next to the fellowships' salaries and the graduate school: 15%, 5-30%.

rows.label: The graduate school's share of the training spending
rows.explainer: Judgment. The St. Jude Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences (founded 2015) admits about a dozen PhD students a year (12 in its first class, 13 in its second) and runs master's programmes in clinical investigation and applied biomedical data science; its students are paid stipends. The master's in Global Child Health trains partner-country clinicians and is part of St. Jude Global. The clinical side (6 haematology-oncology fellows a year, infectious diseases, transplant, neuro-oncology, solid tumour, survivorship and critical care fellows, psychology and pharmacy fellows, nurse residencies, rehabilitation students, rotating residents) is larger: 35%, 20-50%.

rows.label: Global branch: children with cancer treated a year at the partner units St. Jude Global actively supports
rows.explainer: Judgment; St. Jude publishes no count of children reached. 'More than 500 member institutions and foundations around the world have joined the St. Jude Global Alliance', and St. Jude Global 'works directly with providers and institutions in more than 70 countries' (https://global.stjude.org/en-us/about/our-impact.html); a paediatric cancer unit in a middle-income country sees roughly 50 to 300 new patients a year (Ribeiro, Cancer Control 2014, describes a demonstration unit with about 200 new cases a year), and only some members get active programmes (twinning, nurse training, protocol adaptation, pathology support). The children the Global Platform's medicines reach elsewhere are gl_platform_children. Best: about 120 actively supported units at 200 children; low if active support reaches only a few dozen units, high if most members' patients benefit.

rows.label: Global branch: other children reached by the Global Platform's medicines in the year
rows.explainer: Judgment. The Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines, launched with St. Jude's $200 million commitment in February 2025, aims to supply medicines for about 120,000 children over five to seven years in up to 50 countries, starting with six pilot countries (UN News, https://news.un.org/feed/view/en/story/2025/02/1160036): about 20,000 a year at full scale. FY2025 (to June 2025) saw only its first deliveries in the pilots, and some of those children are at units already counted in gl_unit_children: 4,000 more children, 0 to 15,000.

rows.label: Share of new cancer patients who would die within five years under standard US care

source.title: National Cancer Institute, Cancer in Children and Adolescents (fact sheet)
source.quote: 5-year survival was 83.2% for children younger than 1 year, 87.8% for children ages 1–4 years

rows.explainer: US five-year survival for childhood cancer is about 85-88% (2013-2019, by age; 87.3% at 15-19), so 12-15% die. St. Jude's mix has more brain tumours (32% of its new cancer patients) and more referred high-risk cases than the national mix, so 15% (12-20%). The baseline mortality the survival gain below is a share of; it is the rate over a course of treatment, not a yearly rate.

rows.label: Cut in five-year deaths at St. Jude against standard US care, cancer patients (relative)
rows.explainer: Judgment, anchored on the one like-for-like comparison: in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, St. Jude's Total XV trial (2000-07, 498 patients) reached 93.5% ± 1.9% five-year survival against 90.4% ± 0.5% in the Children's Oncology Group's trials (2000-05, 7,153 patients; Pui et al., J Clin Oncol 2015, Table 1, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4567699/): deaths 6.5% against 9.6%, a third fewer. The other leading groups sit between (DFCI 91%, UKALL 91.6%). For the whole cancer mix a quarter fewer deaths: brain and solid tumours (two-thirds of St. Jude's cancer patients) have no comparable published comparison, and nine in ten US children with cancer are treated at Children's Oncology Group centres on the same or similar protocols, many developed at St. Jude. 0 if the gap is case mix; 40% if the solid-tumour and brain-tumour programmes (proton therapy, its own neuro-oncology trials) do as well as leukaemia's best. How far the comparison is confounded is in internal_validity_adj, not here.

rows.label: Share of other new patients (blood disorders, sickle cell, HIV) who would die within five years under standard US care
rows.explainer: Judgment. Most of these children have non-malignant blood disorders, sickle cell disease or HIV, with five-year mortality of a few per cent in US care; a minority have bone-marrow failure or immune disorders treated by transplant, with higher risk.

rows.explainer: Judgment: less than the cancer cut, since sickle cell and HIV care follow national guidelines St. Jude shares with other centres; 0 to 30% (transplant outcomes).

rows.label: Share of children at supported partner hospitals who would die without the partnership's improvements
rows.explainer: Judgment. Survival from childhood cancer is about 20-30% in low-income countries ('an overwhelming 70 per cent death rate', UN News on the Global Platform's launch, https://news.un.org/feed/view/en/story/2025/02/1160036) and more than 80% in high-income ones; St. Jude's partners are mostly referral hospitals in middle-income countries, where 40-60% survive.

rows.label: Cut in deaths at supported partner hospitals from the partnership (relative)
rows.explainer: Judgment. The published before-and-after results of St. Jude's twinnings: in Recife, Brazil, five-year event-free survival from acute lymphoblastic leukaemia rose from 32% (1980-89) to 63% (1997-2002) among 375 children, with abandonment of treatment within a year falling from 16% to 0.5% (Howard et al., JAMA 2004;291:2471-5, https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.291.20.2471); events there count relapse, toxic death and abandonment, so deaths fell by less than the 46% drop in events. St. Jude's goal for a new partner is 'to quickly achieve a 60% event-free survival rate', from rates that start below 10% to 60% depending on the country (Ribeiro, Cancer Control 2014, https://www.cancercontrol.info/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/106-110-Ribeiro.pdf). These are the intensive, long twinnings of the first 19 sites, for leukaemia, the most curable cancer; the average Alliance member now gets lighter support (training, protocols, consultations, medicines) for all its cancers. No results at other partner sites are published that would make a reference class across partners; Ribeiro notes that acute myeloid leukaemia and brain tumours 'remain challenging at many partner sites'. 12% fewer deaths on average (6 points at a 50% baseline), 2% for light support of units treating mostly hard cancers, 30% for twinnings like Recife. Before the counterfactual (the background trend) and the evidence discount. It counts better delivery of today's standard care at partner units (protocols adapted, abandonment, supportive care, medicines); gains from new treatments the research produces are credited in the research model, not here.

rows.label: Clinical training branch: cut in their patients' deaths from training at St. Jude rather than elsewhere (relative)
rows.explainer: Judgment on the literature on where doctors trained and their patients' later outcomes. A systematic review of residency training and patient outcomes found 'limited evidence' on the effect on later practice, with one study linking outcomes back to the training site (van der Leeuw et al., BMC Medicine 2012, https://doi.org/10.1186/1741-7015-10-65). Among 454 surgeons from 73 programmes, patients of surgeons from top-tertile programmes had 9.68% complications against 10.79% from bottom-tertile ones (about 10% fewer, shrinking with years in practice) but almost the same in-hospital death rate, 0.483% against 0.476% (Bansal et al., JAMA Surgery 2016, https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2015.3637). St. Jude against the programme a fellow would otherwise attend is less than top against bottom, and the effect on deaths is smaller than on complications: 1% fewer deaths, 0 as the surgical death rates suggest, 4% at half the complications gap.

rows.label: Clinical training branch: deaths averted per trainee over a career, discounted
rows.explainer: Patients a year × baseline deaths × the cut, over the years of practice, each year discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Clinical training branch: years from the year's training to the trainees' practice
rows.explainer: Judgment: the year's spending trains fellows in every year of a three-year fellowship; on average they finish about a year and a half later.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: years from the year's training to graduation
rows.explainer: Judgment: the year's spending trains students in every year of a five- to six-year PhD; on average they graduate about three years later.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: years a graduate works in research
rows.explainer: Judgment: a career of 30-35 years, of which many PhD graduates spend part or all outside research; NIH postdoctoral fellowships raised the chance of later research awards by 4.0-6.3 percentage points (Heggeness et al., PLOS ONE 2023, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0272230), so retention in research is far from certain. 15 years (6-25).

rows.label: Graduate school branch: research spending a researcher's year of work directs
rows.explainer: Judgment: an NIH research project grant pays about $600,000 a year in total costs for a principal investigator's laboratory of three to five researchers; industry research costs more per researcher. $250,000 a researcher-year.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: extra research output from St. Jude's training over training elsewhere
rows.explainer: Judgment anchored on the nearest causal estimate of what better-resourced training adds: a regression-discontinuity study of NIH postdoctoral fellowships found 'about one additional publication over the next five years, which reflects a 20 percent increase in research productivity' (Jacob and Lefgren, Research Policy 2011, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2011.04.003). Most of St. Jude's students would earn a PhD elsewhere, so what the school adds is the difference in training, which a fellowship (funding and freedom) overstates: half of it, 10%, 2-25%.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: healthy years a dollar of medical research brings, undiscounted, once in practice
rows.explainer: Judgment on the returns-to-research literature: Glover et al. (BMC Medicine 2014, https://doi.org/10.1186/1741-7015-12-99) put UK public and charity cancer research at £15 billion over 1970-2009 (2011/12 prices) and the QALYs gained from cancer care 1991-2010 at 5.9 million, 17% of their net value attributable to UK research, with a lag of about 15 years: about 1 million QALYs from the research of roughly 1976-1995, about a third of the £15 billion if spending grew steadily (about £5 billion, our reading, not the paper's figure), some 2e-4 QALYs per 2011/12 pound, about 1e-4 per 2024 dollar undiscounted. Cardiovascular and mental-health research earned health-gain returns of about 9% and 7% a year (Health Economics Research Group, Office of Health Economics and RAND Europe, 2008). Cross-check: the research model's cancer chain gives about 8e-5 a dollar undiscounted after its evidence step (st-jude-charityevals-research, field_dalys_per_dollar before the wait). The wait is gs_years_until_effect. Glover counts the UK's health gains only, so the return is low for research whose results travel, as St. Jude's do; the evidence adjustment doesn't add to it for that.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: years from the research to its health gains
rows.explainer: Judgment on the translation lag: about 17 years from research to practice (Morris, Wooding and Grant, J R Soc Med 2011, https://doi.org/10.1258/jrsm.2011.110180), 15 for UK cancer research (Glover et al. 2014); 12 (6-17), the same as the research model's cancer branch, since graduates do the same mix of basic and clinical research.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: healthy years per graduate, discounted
rows.formula: pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, gs_research_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -(gs_years_to_graduate + gs_years_until_effect) * gs_research_spend_per_year * gs_productivity_uplift * gs_dalys_per_research_dollar
rows.explainer: The research a graduate directs over a career × the extra output the training brings × the health return of research, every year and the waits before them discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: share of the health gains that is illness averted
rows.explainer: The graduates' research is mostly on childhood cancer and catastrophic childhood diseases, so its health gains split like childhood cancer's burden: illness kept as healthy years, the rest deaths (decision 2026-10-31 #4).

rows.label: Graduate school branch: deaths averted per healthy year gained
rows.explainer: Turns the return's healthy years back into the deaths behind them, so each is valued by age at the site's value of a death.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: value of a death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the ages of childhood cancer deaths, times your multiplier on the value of a life. Times the survivors' remaining-life share (survivor_life_share). Glover et al.'s returns already count some of survivors' shorter lives, so the ratio may overlap a little here (the branch is about 5% of the result); kept so every death is valued one way.

rows.label: Community branch: rise in HPV vaccination among adolescents whose clinicians are trained (percentage points)
rows.explainer: Read as percentage points: the review pools vaccination rates in the trial arms, and its abstract reports the gain in vaccination 'rates'; the full text (MDPI) wasn't reachable to confirm it is a risk difference, and a relative 5.2% would make this branch, under 0.1% of the result, smaller still. Six US randomised trials with 245,195 adolescents: 5.2 points on average, 2.3 for passive conversational techniques, 11.4 with presumptive communication and audit and feedback; the range. A broader review of US interventions found HPV vaccine initiation 1.84 times as likely (95% CI 1.36-2.48; Rodriguez et al., Am J Prev Med 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2018.10.033).

source.title: Chandeying et al., Clinician Communication Training to Increase Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Uptake: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, Vaccines 2024
source.quote: clinician communication training could enhance vaccination uptake rates by an average of 5.2%

rows.label: Community branch: adolescents vaccinated who otherwise wouldn't be, a year
Community branch: deaths a year in the US from cancers HPV causes
rows.explainer: Judgment built on CDC figures (https://www.cdc.gov/hpv/about/cancers-caused-by-hpv.html, retrieved 2026-11-04): about 37,800 HPV-attributable cancers a year (cervical 10,800, throat 14,800, anal 7,200, vulvar, vaginal and penile 4,600) and 'about 4,000 women die from cervical cancer each year'; the other HPV cancers, mostly HPV-positive throat cancers with better survival, kill perhaps a sixth of those diagnosed, about 4,000 more. 8,000 (6,000-11,000).

rows.label: Births in the United States, 2024

source.title: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, FastStats: Births and Natality (Births: Final Data for 2024)

rows.explainer: The size of a birth cohort, to turn deaths a year into a lifetime risk.

rows.label: Community branch: an unvaccinated person's lifetime risk of dying of an HPV cancer
rows.explainer: Deaths a year ÷ a birth cohort (about 0.2%), the steady-state lifetime risk in today's mostly unvaccinated adult population.

rows.label: Community branch: cut in HPV cancer deaths from vaccination in adolescence
rows.explainer: Invasive cervical cancer in 926,362 Swedish girls and women followed up to 18 years, with no sign of waning; the 2020 analysis found 0.12 (Lei et al., NEJM 2020, https://doi.org/10.1056/nejmoa1917338). Applied to every HPV cancer, whose evidence for the other sites is from infection and lesions, not cancer; herd protection of others isn't counted. The interval is the range.

source.title: Wu et al., Extended follow-up of invasive cervical cancer risk after quadrivalent HPV vaccination: nationwide, register based study, The BMJ 2026
source.quote: Among participants vaccinated before 17 years, the overall fully adjusted incidence rate ratios compared with the unvaccinated group was 0.21 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.13 to 0.32)

rows.label: Community branch: years from vaccination to the cancer deaths averted
rows.explainer: Judgment: vaccination at 11-13; HPV cancer deaths come mostly at 45-70.

rows.label: Community branch: share of the deaths averted under 50
rows.explainer: Judgment: cervical cancer deaths come younger (median about 59) than throat and anal cancer deaths; deaths after 75 are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Community branch: the HPV programme's share of the community programmes' spending
rows.explainer: Judgment from the CHNA 2022 list (p. 52): the HPV programme is the one with its own staff and a regional role; the HIV education sessions, school healthy-lifestyle lessons, survivorship forums and transition programmes share the rest.

rows.label: Community branch: what a dollar of the other community activities does, relative to the HPV work
rows.explainer: Judgment. Health education sessions have weak evidence of changing health (the school-based vaccination education meta-analysis found effects on knowledge more than on uptake; Rosso et al., Vaccine 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.128479); the HIV sessions (6,100 people, on PrEP and stigma) and transition support for St. Jude's own survivors may do more. 30% of the HPV work's value per dollar; 0 to as much.

rows.label: Community branch: the other activities, as a multiple of the HPV work's deaths averted
Community branch: HPV cancer deaths averted per adolescent reached
Share of deaths averted under five, deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (us_deaths_averted * us_share_under5 + gl_deaths_averted * gl_share_under5 + tr_deaths_averted * us_share_under5 + gs_deaths_averted * @death_ages.childhood_cancer_share_under5_world) / deaths_averted
rows.explainer: Each branch values its deaths with its own ages; the clinical trainees' patients have the US patients' ages, and no HPV cancer death averted falls under five.

rows.label: Share of deaths over five at 5-14, deaths-weighted average, for reading only
rows.formula: (us_deaths_averted * (1 - us_share_under5) * us_share_5_14_of_over5 + gl_deaths_averted * (1 - gl_share_under5) * gl_share_5_14_of_over5 + tr_deaths_averted * (1 - us_share_under5) * us_share_5_14_of_over5 + gs_deaths_averted * @death_ages.childhood_cancer_share_5_14_world) / (deaths_averted - us_deaths_averted * us_share_under5 - gl_deaths_averted * gl_share_under5 - tr_deaths_averted * us_share_under5 - gs_deaths_averted * @death_ages.childhood_cancer_share_under5_world)
rows.explainer: For reading; each branch uses its own. No HPV cancer death averted falls at 5-14, so the community branch's deaths count only in the denominator.

rows.label: Share of deaths over 15 at 15-49, for reading only
rows.explainer: 1 in the patient care, global and training branches; the HPV deaths averted are mostly at 50 and over.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the value of deaths and income
rows.explainer: 0: illness is counted in DALYs instead (dalys_illness_averted_per_person and the bridge), never both. GiveWell's shares are for prevention in poor countries and don't apply here.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person reached
rows.explainer: 0: a children's hospital doesn't avert stillbirths.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person, ln(consumption) a year
rows.explainer: 0: a survivor's later earnings are part of the value of the life saved (the moral weight); St. Jude's patients aren't a population with evidence of a developmental income effect like malaria or deworming.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: No income gain is counted (ln_income_gain_per_year is 0), so no wait applies; none of the site's figures (malaria, SMC, iron, deworming) fits this programme.

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times. Read by every model that values a long-term income gain (INV-13).

rows.label: Share of new US patients spared a lasting late effect they would have had at another centre
rows.explainer: Judgment. Survivors of childhood cancer carry late effects (heart, hearing, fertility, neurocognitive); St. Jude's proton therapy for brain tumours and its survivorship clinic aim to cut them, but the protocols that reduce late effects (no cranial irradiation in leukaemia, risk-adapted doses) are now standard at other centres too. 3% of patients spared one; 0 if other centres match St. Jude, 10% if proton therapy spares many brain-tumour survivors (a third of cancer patients).

rows.label: Share of the late effects spared that are hearing loss
rows.explainer: Judgment: platinum chemotherapy and cranial radiation cause hearing loss in many survivors of brain tumours and solid tumours, the largest group St. Jude's proton therapy and dose reductions aim at.

rows.label: Share of the late effects spared that are heart failure
rows.explainer: Judgment: anthracycline cardiotoxicity, which cardioprotection and lower cumulative doses reduce; the rest are neurocognitive effects (mild intellectual disability).

rows.label: Disability weight of a typical late effect
rows.explainer: The GBD 2019 disability weights of the commonest late effects (shared facts), mixed by the shares above.

rows.label: Years a late effect lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment: from the end of treatment in childhood through most of adult life; discounted in us_dalys_illness_per_patient.

rows.label: Illness averted per new US patient over standard care, in DALYs
rows.explainer: Patients spared × the disability weight × the years it would have lasted, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Healthy years from illness averted and research per person reached (for reading)
rows.explainer: The US branch's late effects and the graduate school's research, over the people reached, for reading; the bridge uses each branch's own figure.

rows.label: What a family would pay out of pocket in a year of treatment elsewhere (medical bills, travel, lodging, food), 2018 dollars

source.title: Iragorri et al., The Out-of-Pocket Cost Burden of Cancer Care: A Systematic Literature Review, Current Oncology 2021

rows.explainer: St. Jude bills no family and pays travel, housing and meals for the patient and a parent. At another hospital a family pays deductibles and co-payments (none for the 41% on Medicaid) and its own travel and lodging. The review gives paediatric cancer patients USD 800 a month, pooled across high-income countries (2018 dollars; likely low for the US, where adult patients and caregivers spend $180 to $2,600 a month): $800 × 12 = $9,600 a family-year of active treatment, $3,000 (Medicaid families near the centre) to $20,000. Lost parental earnings aren't counted, since St. Jude doesn't replace them either.

rows.label: The same, in 2024 dollars
rows.explainer: In the prices of the year modelled (Convention 8), US consumer prices (World Bank).

rows.label: Years of active treatment the family costs cover
rows.explainer: Judgment: leukaemia treatment lasts 2-3 years (most of it outpatient), solid and brain tumours about a year, other patients' care is lighter; 1.5 years on average.

rows.label: Share of those costs no one else would have covered
rows.explainer: Judgment: at other centres some families get help with lodging (Ronald McDonald Houses), travel and bills from hospital financial counselling and childhood-cancer charities; 70% of the costs would have stayed with the family.

rows.label: Consumption gain per family member in a treatment year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: The family's saving as a share of an average US household's consumption by the household survey (2.4 people at the Consumer Expenditure Survey's $32,723 each, 2024), on the site's one log scale. The saving is valued like cash (the cash-income family's chain). Changed 2026-11-04 (docs/normalization.md, consumption baselines): the base is the household survey of the people served, the Consumer Expenditure Survey's $32,723 a person in 2024, not the national accounts' $58,517, which also count imputed rents, employer- and government-paid health care and non-profits' spending. A shared conversion, not thin data.

rows.label: US branch: evidence adjustment on the survival gain
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: External validity (US branch): the comparison's setting against St. Jude's today
rows.explainer: 1: the comparison is between US centres treating US children, the setting of this branch; how far the trials measured a real difference is in internal_validity_adj.

rows.label: Internal validity (US branch): how far the comparison measures St. Jude's own effect
rows.explainer: Judgment. The survival gain comes from comparing trials run by different groups, not from randomising children between centres: St. Jude's trial patients may differ from the Children's Oncology Group's in risk and in who enrols. GiveWell's internal-validity adjustments for randomised trials run from 0.73 (syphilis treatment) to 0.95 (malaria trials) (@givewell_common.internal_validity_adjustment_*); a non-randomised comparison between study groups is well below them: 0.6, 1 if the 3-point gap is all St. Jude's care.

rows.label: US branch: share of the gain that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the survival gain is already the difference from the care these children would otherwise get (other US centres), so nothing more is taken off for what would have happened anyway (Convention 5).

rows.label: US branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind the care
rows.explainer: St. Jude's own funds ÷ the full cost of care; insurers paid the rest (Convention 2). Their payments buy care these children would get elsewhere anyway, which the survival gain already nets out, so a higher share is arguable; 81% follows the site's rule.

rows.label: US branch: share of patients counted who get the care as studied
rows.explainer: 1: the patients counted are the patients St. Jude treated.

rows.label: Would others have paid for this anyway (below 1), or does the money pull others in (above 1)?
rows.explainer: Judgment. No government or other funder would step in for St. Jude's own funds; its reserves (gift_to_grant_years) are counted as a wait, not as funging. 0.9 if the reserves mean a marginal donation mostly substitutes for investment returns St. Jude would spend anyway.

rows.label: Global branch: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Judgment on the validity of the before-and-after evidence itself: published series are the ones that went well (publication selection), and event-free survival counts relapse and abandonment, so deaths fell by less than events (allowed for in gl_mortality_reduction, as is the step from the flagship twinnings to the average partner). The background trend a before-and-after comparison can't separate is in gl_counterfactual_adj, so it isn't taken off here. 0.6, as the US branch's non-randomised comparison (internal_validity_adj); 0.3 if the published series are a best-case subset, 0.9 if not.

rows.label: Global branch: share of the improvement that wouldn't have come anyway with no partnership at all
rows.explainer: Judgment: the background trend only. Survival from childhood cancer in middle-income countries rises over a partnership's decade without any partner too, with national cancer plans, health spending and economic growth; about 30% of the improvement at partner units would have come anyway. Other partners' and local funders' contributions are not taken off here: they are resources behind the improvement, in gl_attribution_share (Convention 5, one question per adjustment).

rows.label: Global branch: local and government spending per child treated at a partner hospital (2018 US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment, anchored on the costing studies in the systematic review of childhood cancer treatment in low- and middle-income countries (Fung et al., BMJ Global Health 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830048/): for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in middle-income countries about $5,700 a patient (Bangladesh), $9,300-16,900 (Iran), $21,000-24,800 (Mexico) and $8,000-50,000 (China); for all cancers about $10,500 (Ghana) and $30,000 (El Salvador) per newly diagnosed patient a year (the review converted every cost to 2018 US$). $10,000 for the partner units' mix; $3,000 for lower-middle-income units, $25,000 for upper-middle-income units on full leukaemia protocols. A check: St. Jude's own direct financial contribution falls to about a few per cent of a mature partner unit's budget (Ribeiro, Cancer Control 2014, https://www.cancercontrol.info/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/106-110-Ribeiro.pdf), though it is the largest part at the start, and St. Jude's staff time comes on top.

rows.label: Global branch: local and government spending per child treated, in 2024 prices
rows.explainer: The review's 2018 dollars in the prices of the year modelled (Convention 8), US consumer prices, since the costs are in US dollars.

rows.label: Other international partners' spending per child at the same hospitals (other twinning centres, NGOs, drug donations)
rows.explainer: Judgment: other high-income twinning partners (European and Canadian centres, SIOP programmes), international NGOs and drug donation programmes also support many St. Jude partner units, with smaller budgets than St. Jude Global's; about a tenth of local spending. Anchor: St. Jude's own direct financial contribution falls to a few per cent of a mature unit's budget (Ribeiro 2014), and other external donors are of the same order or smaller, so $1,000 (about 10% of the $10,000 local cost) allows for several of them; $300 to $3,000. In 2024 dollars, about 8% of gl_local_cost_per_child's 2024 value ($12,500).

rows.label: Global branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind the care at partner hospitals
rows.explainer: St. Jude Global's spending ÷ its spending plus what governments, hospitals, local foundations, families and other international partners spend treating these children (Convention 2). Both sides at direct cost, as in the research model's shares of the field: St. Jude's fundraising and administration (the overhead) are in the cost, not resources behind the care. About 21% at the best guesses. That is far above St. Jude's share of a mature twinning unit's own budget, which Ribeiro (Cancer Control 2014) describes as falling to a few per cent, because St. Jude Global's spending also pays for what never enters a unit's budget: the Memphis-based faculty and staff who consult, train and adapt protocols, the Alliance's central programmes and registries, and the medicines the Global Platform supplies; the share is of all resources behind the children's care, not of the unit's budget.

rows.label: Global branch: share of children counted who get the improved care
rows.explainer: 1: the reach is already the children at actively supported units; how much of the improvement reaches them is in the survival gain.

rows.label: Clinical training branch: trust in the effect
rows.explainer: Judgment on the validity of the training-site studies: they adjust for patients and hospitals but not for which trainees go to which programmes, so part of a strong programme's better outcomes is its stronger recruits (selection). 0.6, as for the other non-randomised comparisons in this model (internal_validity_adj, gl_evidence_adj).

rows.label: Clinical training branch: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the effect is already the difference from training at another programme, which these trainees would otherwise attend (Convention 5).

rows.label: Clinical training branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind the training
rows.explainer: Judgment (Convention 2): the haematology-oncology fellowship is run with the University of Tennessee Health Science Center and Le Bonheur Children's Hospital, where fellows also train, and trainees' own unpaid study hours are an input; St. Jude pays the fellows' salaries.

rows.label: Clinical training branch: delivery as studied
rows.explainer: 1: the trainees counted are the ones trained.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: trust in the effect
rows.explainer: Judgment on the validity of the chain's links: the fellowship effect is a regression-discontinuity estimate (internally sound), but it counts publications, and a publication's share of a field's health return is assumed equal to a research dollar's; the return per research dollar is one country's record. 0.7, the medical-research family's default evidence adjustment (as in the research model, ca_evidence_adj).

rows.label: Graduate school branch: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the uplift is already the difference from training elsewhere (Convention 5).

rows.label: Graduate school branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: 1: the uplift is measured against the same later research funding in both cases, so the funders of graduates' later research share none of it; St. Jude pays the stipends.

rows.label: Graduate school branch: delivery as studied
rows.explainer: 1: the graduates counted are the ones trained.

rows.label: Community branch: trust in the effect
rows.explainer: Judgment on the validity of the evidence: the uptake effect is a meta-analysis of randomised trials and the vaccine effect a large register study against cervical cancer; the effect against the other HPV cancers (half the deaths) is inferred from infection and lesion endpoints. 0.8.

rows.label: Community branch: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment: the trials measured uptake over months to two years; some adolescents in the control groups are vaccinated later (catch-up to 26, at lower effect), and US coverage rises by itself by a point or two a year.

rows.label: Community branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Judgment (Convention 2): the roundtables are coalitions with the American Cancer Society, state health departments, insurers and the clinics, whose staff time does the vaccinating; St. Jude funds the coordination and much of the content.

rows.label: Community branch: delivery as studied
rows.explainer: 1: delivery is in cm_evidence_adj (lighter work than the trials').

rows.label: Cash and investments at 30 June 2025

source.title: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and ALSAC, combined financial statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, Deloitte & Touche LLP)
source.page: p. 3, combined statements of financial position (in 000s)
source.quote: CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS $ 557,709 ... UNRESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 8,444,862 ... RESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 1,587,521

rows.explainer: Cash ($557.7 million), unrestricted investments ($8,444.9 million) and investments restricted by donors ($1,587.5 million): about three and three-quarter years of spending held in reserve.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before St. Jude spends it
rows.explainer: The reserves ÷ a year's spending, as the template asks for a charity that spends from reserves: 3.7 years. St. Jude holds its reserves by policy and spends from donations, bequests and investment returns, so a dollar given today adds to the pool and is, on average, spent about this much later. While it waits it is invested (interest_yield), which almost cancels the discount.

rows.label: Long-run nominal return on the invested reserves
rows.explainer: Judgment. The reserves earned $939.3 million in FY2025 on about $9.6 billion of investments (p. 4; average of the two year-ends, p. 3), 9.7%, and $856.7 million in FY2024: two strong market years. Long-run returns of diversified endowment portfolios have averaged about 6-7% a year nominal over ten-year periods (US college and university endowment studies, NACUBO-Commonfund); 6.5%, 4% in a weak decade, 9% at the recent returns.

rows.label: Yearly rise in the cost of care and research
rows.explainer: Judgment: US medical-care prices have risen about 3% a year over the past two decades (BLS consumer price index for medical care), a little faster than general inflation; what a dollar held in reserve buys later falls by this much a year.

rows.label: Real return on the invested reserves while a donation waits
rows.explainer: The return in what it buys: the benefit a later dollar buys is valued in today's care.

rows.label: Years from the spending to the care
rows.explainer: 0: the spending is the year's care and support itself.

rows.label: Years from treatment to the middle of the deaths averted
rows.explainer: Judgment: the children who would have died without the better care die mostly of relapse or treatment toxicity within five years of diagnosis, more of them early; two years to the middle.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate; the reserves earn their real return while a donation waits (interest_yield).

rows.label: Clinical training branch: the waits, discounted
rows.explainer: The reserves' wait, the time to the trainees' practice and to the middle of each patient's risk, discounted at the shared rate; the years of practice are discounted in tr_deaths_averted_per_trainee.

rows.label: Community branch: the waits, discounted
rows.explainer: The reserves' wait and the decades until the cancer deaths, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until families' costs are covered
rows.explainer: The reserves' wait only: the savings come during treatment, whose years pv_annuity_due already discounts (not at the middle of the deaths averted).

rows.label: US branch: discount for an outcome not measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): St. Jude counts its patients, but the survival gain over other US centres is a judgment on a comparison between trials, not a controlled comparison.

rows.label: GL branch: discount for an outcome not measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: St. Jude publishes no count of children at supported units and no controlled evaluation; reach and effect are judgments.

rows.label: TR branch: discount for an outcome not measured for this charity
